title: Container With Most Water
description: Brute force to optimized: checking every pair versus two pointers always moving the shorter line.

blocks.text: Given an array height where each value represents the height of a vertical line at that position, choose two lines that, together with the x axis, form a container holding the most water. Return the maximum amount of water that container can hold.

blocks.caption: Two pointers from both ends, always moving the pointer at the currently shorter line inward

blocks.text: Given an array height where each value represents the height of a vertical line at that position, choose two lines that, together with the x axis, form a container holding the most water. Return the maximum amount of water that container can hold.

blocks.title: Analogy: Choosing Two Fence Posts to Hold Back the Most Water
blocks.text: Like choosing two fence posts of different heights along a line to form a temporary basin, where the amount of water held depends on both how far apart the posts are and how tall the shorter of the two is, since water can never rise above the shorter post.

blocks.caption: Pick two lines whose width and shorter height together hold the most water

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["Lines at index 1 (height 8) and index 8 (height 7)","width 7, height min(8, 7) equals 7, area 49","The water level can never rise above the shorter of the two chosen lines, so height 7, not 8, caps the area, multiplied by the width of 7 positions between them"],["No other pair produces a larger area","this is the maximum","Every other combination of two lines produces a smaller width, a smaller capping height, or both"],["Answer","49","7 times 7 is the largest area achievable from any pair in this array"]]}

{"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["Only one possible pair, width 1, height min(1, 1) equals 1","area 1","With exactly two lines, there is only one possible pair to consider at all"],["Answer","1","The single available pair's area is trivially both the minimum and the maximum"]]}

blocks.text: Edge case: heights strictly decreasing, like [5, 4, 3, 2, 1]

Even though the tallest line sits at the very start, the best container still depends on balancing width against the shorter of the two chosen lines: pairing index 0 (height 5) with index 2 (height 3) gives width 2 and a capping height of 3, an area of 6, which turns out to be the true maximum for this array, larger than what pairing the two tallest or two most widely spaced lines alone would suggest, giving 6.

Before checking every pair, notice the area formula itself, width times the shorter height, sets up a direct tension: starting from the two widest-apart lines guarantees the largest possible width, but moving either pointer inward can only ever shrink that width, so the only way a move could still help is if it also increases the capping height enough to compensate.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: For any two lines, the area is entirely determined by their distance apart, the width, and whichever of the two is shorter, the height, since water can never rise above the shorter line without spilling over it.

Observation 2: Starting with the two outermost lines gives the maximum possible width immediately, and every subsequent move can only shrink that width further, so any move must be justified by a real chance of a taller capping height.

Observation 3: If the shorter of the two current lines is kept in place and the taller one is moved inward instead, the width shrinks while the capping height stays exactly the same, still limited by the same shorter line, guaranteeing a strictly worse or equal area, an option that can therefore be safely discarded without ever checking it.

Observation 4: Moving the shorter line inward, by contrast, discards exactly that one line while giving every remaining line a chance to be taller, the only move that could possibly raise the capping height enough to beat the current best despite the smaller width.

Whenever an area or capacity depends on a limiting factor, like the shorter of two heights, and a shrinking factor, like width, always move the side responsible for the limiting factor, since keeping it while shrinking the other factor can never improve the result.

This exchange argument, proving that one specific move is always at least as good as its alternative, is what justifies discarding huge numbers of pairs without ever explicitly comparing them, turning an all-pairs search into a single directed sweep.
Check every pair of lines directly, computing the area each pair would form and tracking the largest one found.

items: For every pair of indices i and j, compute the width as j minus i and the height as the shorter of height[i] and height[j].
Compute the area as width times height, and keep the largest area found.

codes.python:
def max_area(height):
    best = 0
    n = len(height)
    for i in range(n):                                        # every pair is checked directly
        for j in range(i + 1, n):
            width = j - i
            area = width * min(height[i], height[j])
            best = max(best, area)
    return best


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(max_area([1, 8, 6, 2, 5, 4, 8, 3, 7]))

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: width is computed as j minus i directly, since the x axis distance between two chosen lines is exactly the difference of their indices, regardless of what lies between them.

The shorter of the two heights is used as the capping height, not the average or the taller value, since water poured between two lines of different heights can never rise above the shorter one without spilling over its edge.
best is updated with the running maximum after every single pair's area is computed, since any pair, not just adjacent or extreme ones, could in principle be the true maximum.

blocks.text: Every pair of lines is directly checked, so the true maximum area is guaranteed to be found.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared), checking every pair.
Space: O(1) extra.

Limitation: most pairs are irrelevant. Once the two outermost lines are considered, moving the taller one inward can never help, the width only shrinks and the height is still capped by the shorter line, so many pairs can be skipped entirely without checking them.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: Checking every pair treats each one as independently unpredictable, but the two outermost lines already guarantee the widest possible container, so every other candidate pair necessarily has a smaller or equal width. That means any candidate that could still beat the current best must compensate for its smaller width with a taller capping height, a strictly narrower condition than "just try everything". Starting from the two ends and always discarding whichever line is currently the shorter one, since keeping it while narrowing the width can only ever hurt, guarantees that every discarded pair really could never have been better than one already considered, collapsing an O(n squared) all-pairs search into a single O(n) sweep that only ever considers pairs that had a genuine chance of improving the answer.

Use two pointers starting at the two ends of the array. Compute the area for the current pair, then move whichever pointer points to the shorter line inward, since that shorter line is the limiting factor and keeping it while shrinking the width could only ever produce a smaller or equal area; only moving the shorter line gives any chance of finding a taller line that might improve the result.
Two pointers from both ends, always moving the pointer at the currently shorter line inward.

blocks.caption: Optimized: two pointers from both ends, always moving the shorter line inward

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), the pointers together traverse the array at most once.
Space: O(1) extra.

Every time the shorter line is moved inward and discarded, it is provably impossible for that exact line, paired with anything on the other side of its current partner, to ever produce a better area than what pairing it with its current partner already achieved, since its own height is already the limiting factor and every other candidate on that side is at most as far away. This means no potentially-optimal pair is ever skipped, only pairs that are mathematically guaranteed to be no better than one already checked, so the true maximum is still found despite never comparing most of the n squared possible pairs directly.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Situation","Why the shorter line can be safely discarded"],"rows":[["The left line is shorter","Every pair pairing this same left line with a different right line inside the current range is at most as wide and still capped by this same shorter left height, so none could beat the current pair"],["The right line is shorter (or tied)","Symmetrically, discarding the right line is safe for the same reason, with left and right roles swapped"]]}

items: width is recomputed every iteration as right minus left, since the range between the two pointers shrinks by exactly one position every time either pointer moves.
The current area is computed and compared against best before deciding which pointer to move, since every valid pair, including the very first one, must be considered as a candidate for the maximum.
Comparing the two heights determines which single pointer advances, moving only the one at the currently shorter line, never both at once.
The loop condition left less than right guarantees the scan terminates exactly when every pair has either been directly checked or safely proven no better than one that was.

blocks.text: The correctness of always moving the shorter line rests on a small but important argument: keeping the shorter line while narrowing the width can never produce a better area, since both the width and the capping height would only get worse or stay the same, so the only line worth ever moving is the current bottleneck.

items: Moving the taller line instead of the shorter one, which throws away potentially better pairs since the shorter line remains the bottleneck regardless of which side is moved.
Forgetting to compute and compare the area before moving a pointer, which would skip checking some valid pairs, including possibly the very first one, entirely.

Assuming the optimal answer must involve the two tallest lines in the array, when in fact width and height trade off against each other, meaning a pair of moderately tall, widely spaced lines can beat a pair of very tall but close-together ones.

items: State the "moving the shorter line is always safe" argument explicitly out loud, since it is exactly the kind of exchange argument interviewers want to hear reasoned through, not just applied.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Maximize an area or capacity limited by the smaller of two values, with a distance factor that shrinks as you narrow the search" points toward two pointers from both ends, always moving the side responsible for the current limiting value.

items: How would you prove the exchange argument rigorously, not just intuitively? Fix the shorter line at some position; every candidate partner on the far side of its current partner has a width no larger than the current pair's width and is still capped by the same shorter height, so no such candidate could ever exceed the current area.

What if the containers needed to hold a minimum amount of water, not maximum? The same two-pointer structure no longer directly applies, since minimizing typically wants the narrowest valid container, a fundamentally different search, often just the smallest adjacent gap.

How does this relate to Trapping Rain Water? Trapping Rain Water asks for the total water trapped across the entire array, not the single best pair of walls, requiring a different technique, prefix and suffix maximum heights, or a two-pointer variant tracking both sides' running maximums, rather than this problem's single best-pair search.
Same "two pointers from both ends, discard the provably worse side" exchange-argument structure as Two Sum II, just with an area-maximizing goal instead of a sum-matching one.
Direct conceptual ancestor of Trapping Rain Water, which extends the same "shorter side is the bottleneck" insight to accumulate water across an entire array rather than just the single best pair.

Same "starting from the extremes guarantees one factor is maximized, so only the other factor needs improving" reasoning as Squares of a Sorted Array's valley-shape exploitation, applied here to width instead of magnitude.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(n squared) time, O(1) space.
Optimized: O(n) time, O(1) space.

items: Pattern: Two pointers converging from both ends, always discarding the line that is currently the shorter, limiting one
Core Idea: Starting from the widest possible container, only moving the pointer at the shorter line can ever improve the area, since keeping it while narrowing the width can only ever hurt or tie
Time: O(n)
Space: O(1)

Most Important Observation: When a result depends on a limiting factor and a shrinking factor together, always move the side responsible for the limiting factor, since the alternative is provably never better
Interview Difficulty: Medium
One-line memory trick: The shorter wall is the problem; move it, not the taller one
